results.title: The kiss of death game ! MARIO ELIE highlights game 7 1995 semi finals vs Phoenix
results.description:
26:00min 2/5FG .400 1/3 3PTS .333 3/3FT 1.000  2RBDS 1ASSIST 5PF 
8 PTS
New York Time : 1995 N.B.A. PLAYOFFS; Rockets Retire Suns, And Maybe Barkley
The Houston Rockets are on their ninth life, and Charles Barkley is about to get a life. A 3-point bomb from Houston's most obscure guard put the Rockets in victory lane today, and it also may have nudged one of basketball's most irascible players out the door.

His left knee creaks, his outside shot is flat and his Phoenix Suns revolve around somebody else, so Barkley announced late this afternoon that his retirement is imminent. He has said all of this before -- annually, in fact -- but today he went so far as to call a post-game meeting to tell his teammates that they can have his locker.

"I'm not saying this is 100 percent done, but I'll say more than likely I have played my last game," said Barkley, 32. "It's just time. It's time. I can't see my skills getting better; I can only see them getting worse."

Today, point guard Kevin Johnson borrowed the Suns from Barkley, scored 46 points, but watched in horror as the Rockets performed yet another magic trick to win, 115-114, in the seventh and final game of this Western Conference semifinal.

Mario Elie, who honed his shot at a park on the corner of 99th and Amsterdam in New York, stole the series by draining a 3-point corner shot with 7.1 seconds remaining.

"I told him he's a wicked man," Houston center Hakeem Olajuwon said of Elie.

It turned a 110-110 tie into a 113-110 Rockets lead and, after a Ping-Pong game of free throws, Danny Ainge's halfcourt heave at the buzzer -- to win it for Phoenix -- found only backboard.



Olajuwon was that center today, scoring 16 of his 29 points in the fourth quarter -- after serving as an assistant coach in the third. Not many clubs are as resilient as Houston. Two players in this series -- Clyde Drexler and Sam Cassell -- have needed I.V. treatment just to play, and two others -- the sharpshooter Vernon Maxwell (leave of absence) and power forward Carl Herrera (shoulder surgery) -- were watching back home.

"We could've gave up a lot of times," guard Kenny Smith said. "We could've given up today."

Instead, they defeated a team that had led this series by 3-1 and a player (A. C. Green) who had guaranteed victory after Game 4.

"Well, I have no words today," Green said. "It didn't happen. I've never experienced it before, so now I have something to describe in my next book."

Speaking of books, the Rockets will be inscribed in the league's history journal. They became only the fifth team to overcome a 3-1 deficit and the first team since the 1982 Sixers (who won in Boston) to win a seventh game on the road.

"Best team won," Phoenix's Johnson said. "We didn't deserve it. What's the excuse now? There is none, not when a team beats you three in a row, including twice at home."

Phoenix's halftime lead was 51-41, but Barkley had left the second quarter prematurely with a sore knee and reportedly took two shots of painkiller. He had started swiftly, with 8 points and 7 rebounds in the first quarter, but, in the second half, the most peculiar discussion occurred: Coach Paul Westphal told Ainge to tell Barkley that Johnson would be clearing out and going one on one against Smith on every possession.

Barkley rolled his eyes, but middle age was obviously setting in.

The third quarter was actually sailing along nicely -- the Suns were leading, 68-59, with Olajuwon on the bench with 5 minutes 25 seconds remaining -- when Drexler (29 points) awoke.

A 22-11 surge by Houston for the remainder of the quarter redirected the course of the game, and Coach Rudy Tomjanovich not once asked Olajuwon to budge.

"It gave me hope for the fourth quarter," Olajuwon said. "They'd taken us this far, and hopefully I could finish it."

Houston led, 81-79, entering the final quarter, and the only possession Olajuwon did not touch the ball was in the final 10 seconds. Phoenix was covering straight up with Joe Kleine or Danny Schayes, and Olajuwon was frothing at the mouth. He scored on fadeaways and layups -- until Phoenix had no choice but to triple-team him in the final two minutes.

The Houston Rockets are on their ninth life, and Charles Barkley is about to get a life. A 3-point bomb from Houston's most obscure guard put the Rockets in victory lane today, and it also may have nudged one of basketball's most irascible players out the door.

results.description:

New York Time : 1995 N.B.A. PLAYOFFS; Rockets Retire Suns, And Maybe Barkley
The Houston Rockets are on their ninth life, and Charles Barkley is about to get a life. A 3-point bomb from Houston's most obscure guard put the Rockets in victory lane today, and it also may have nudged one of basketball's most irascible players out the door.

His left knee creaks, his outside shot is flat and his Phoenix Suns revolve around somebody else, so Barkley announced late this afternoon that his retirement is imminent. He has said all of this before -- annually, in fact -- but today he went so far as to call a post-game meeting to tell his teammates that they can have his locker.

"I'm not saying this is 100 percent done, but I'll say more than likely I have played my last game," said Barkley, 32. "It's just time. It's time. I can't see my skills getting better; I can only see them getting worse."

Today, point guard Kevin Johnson borrowed the Suns from Barkley, scored 46 points, but watched in horror as the Rockets performed yet another magic trick to win, 115-114, in the seventh and final game of this Western Conference semifinal.

Mario Elie, who honed his shot at a park on the corner of 99th and Amsterdam in New York, stole the series by draining a 3-point corner shot with 7.1 seconds remaining.

"I told him he's a wicked man," Houston center Hakeem Olajuwon said of Elie.

It turned a 110-110 tie into a 113-110 Rockets lead and, after a Ping-Pong game of free throws, Danny Ainge's halfcourt heave at the buzzer -- to win it for Phoenix -- found only backboard.



Olajuwon was that center today, scoring 16 of his 29 points in the fourth quarter -- after serving as an assistant coach in the third. Not many clubs are as resilient as Houston. Two players in this series -- Clyde Drexler and Sam Cassell -- have needed I.V. treatment just to play, and two others -- the sharpshooter Vernon Maxwell (leave of absence) and power forward Carl Herrera (shoulder surgery) -- were watching back home.

"We could've gave up a lot of times," guard Kenny Smith said. "We could've given up today."

Instead, they defeated a team that had led this series by 3-1 and a player (A. C. Green) who had guaranteed victory after Game 4.

"Well, I have no words today," Green said. "It didn't happen. I've never experienced it before, so now I have something to describe in my next book."

Speaking of books, the Rockets will be inscribed in the league's history journal. They became only the fifth team to overcome a 3-1 deficit and the first team since the 1982 Sixers (who won in Boston) to win a seventh game on the road.

"Best team won," Phoenix's Johnson said. "We didn't deserve it. What's the excuse now? There is none, not when a team beats you three in a row, including twice at home."

Phoenix's halftime lead was 51-41, but Barkley had left the second quarter prematurely with a sore knee and reportedly took two shots of painkiller. He had started swiftly, with 8 points and 7 rebounds in the first quarter, but, in the second half, the most peculiar discussion occurred: Coach Paul Westphal told Ainge to tell Barkley that Johnson would be clearing out and going one on one against Smith on every possession.

Barkley rolled his eyes, but middle age was obviously setting in.

The third quarter was actually sailing along nicely -- the Suns were leading, 68-59, with Olajuwon on the bench with 5 minutes 25 seconds remaining -- when Drexler (29 points) awoke.

A 22-11 surge by Houston for the remainder of the quarter redirected the course of the game, and Coach Rudy Tomjanovich not once asked Olajuwon to budge.

"It gave me hope for the fourth quarter," Olajuwon said. "They'd taken us this far, and hopefully I could finish it."

Houston led, 81-79, entering the final quarter, and the only possession Olajuwon did not touch the ball was in the final 10 seconds. Phoenix was covering straight up with Joe Kleine or Danny Schayes, and Olajuwon was frothing at the mouth. He scored on fadeaways and layups -- until Phoenix had no choice but to triple-team him in the final two minutes.

With 45 seconds left, Smith made two free throws to elevate Houston to a 110-109 lead, but Phoenix's Johnson was kneed and fouled after rebounding a Dan Majerle miss. He made the first foul shot with 21.6 seconds left -- his 21st in a row -- but missed the second.

Houston called time out with 20.4 seconds left and, when Phoenix trapped at midcourt, the ball was swung whimsically to Elie open in the corner. Schayes was the closest defender, guarding Olajuwon -- "It was either give up the jumper or let Hakeem have a dunk," Schayes said -- and so he let Elie airmail it.

"I've hit bigger shots," Elie said later. "Nah, just kidding."

results.title: 10pts/4assists/2rbds KENNY SMITH Game 7 1995 semi finals vs Phoenix SUNS
results.description:
32min, 3/8 FG, 1/4 3pts, 3/4 FT, 2 Def rbds, 4 assists, 2 TOV, 5 PF, 10PTS
New York Time : 1995 N.B.A. PLAYOFFS; Rockets Retire Suns, And Maybe Barkley
The Houston Rockets are on their ninth life, and Charles Barkley is about to get a life. A 3-point bomb from Houston's most obscure guard put the Rockets in victory lane today, and it also may have nudged one of basketball's most irascible players out the door.

His left knee creaks, his outside shot is flat and his Phoenix Suns revolve around somebody else, so Barkley announced late this afternoon that his retirement is imminent. He has said all of this before -- annually, in fact -- but today he went so far as to call a post-game meeting to tell his teammates that they can have his locker.

"I'm not saying this is 100 percent done, but I'll say more than likely I have played my last game," said Barkley, 32. "It's just time. It's time. I can't see my skills getting better; I can only see them getting worse."

Today, point guard Kevin Johnson borrowed the Suns from Barkley, scored 46 points, but watched in horror as the Rockets performed yet another magic trick to win, 115-114, in the seventh and final game of this Western Conference semifinal.

Mario Elie, who honed his shot at a park on the corner of 99th and Amsterdam in New York, stole the series by draining a 3-point corner shot with 7.1 seconds remaining.

"I told him he's a wicked man," Houston center Hakeem Olajuwon said of Elie.

It turned a 110-110 tie into a 113-110 Rockets lead and, after a Ping-Pong game of free throws, Danny Ainge's halfcourt heave at the buzzer -- to win it for Phoenix -- found only backboard.



Olajuwon was that center today, scoring 16 of his 29 points in the fourth quarter -- after serving as an assistant coach in the third. Not many clubs are as resilient as Houston. Two players in this series -- Clyde Drexler and Sam Cassell -- have needed I.V. treatment just to play, and two others -- the sharpshooter Vernon Maxwell (leave of absence) and power forward Carl Herrera (shoulder surgery) -- were watching back home.

"We could've gave up a lot of times," guard Kenny Smith said. "We could've given up today."

Instead, they defeated a team that had led this series by 3-1 and a player (A. C. Green) who had guaranteed victory after Game 4.

"Well, I have no words today," Green said. "It didn't happen. I've never experienced it before, so now I have something to describe in my next book."

Speaking of books, the Rockets will be inscribed in the league's history journal. They became only the fifth team to overcome a 3-1 deficit and the first team since the 1982 Sixers (who won in Boston) to win a seventh game on the road.

"Best team won," Phoenix's Johnson said. "We didn't deserve it. What's the excuse now? There is none, not when a team beats you three in a row, including twice at home."

Phoenix's halftime lead was 51-41, but Barkley had left the second quarter prematurely with a sore knee and reportedly took two shots of painkiller. He had started swiftly, with 8 points and 7 rebounds in the first quarter, but, in the second half, the most peculiar discussion occurred: Coach Paul Westphal told Ainge to tell Barkley that Johnson would be clearing out and going one on one against Smith on every possession.

Barkley rolled his eyes, but middle age was obviously setting in.

The third quarter was actually sailing along nicely -- the Suns were leading, 68-59, with Olajuwon on the bench with 5 minutes 25 seconds remaining -- when Drexler (29 points) awoke.

A 22-11 surge by Houston for the remainder of the quarter redirected the course of the game, and Coach Rudy Tomjanovich not once asked Olajuwon to budge.

"It gave me hope for the fourth quarter," Olajuwon said. "They'd taken us this far, and hopefully I could finish it."

Houston led, 81-79, entering the final quarter, and the only possession Olajuwon did not touch the ball was in the final 10 seconds. Phoenix was covering straight up with Joe Kleine or Danny Schayes, and Olajuwon was frothing at the mouth. He scored on fadeaways and layups -- until Phoenix had no choice but to triple-team him in the final two minutes.

With 45 seconds left, Smith made two free throws to elevate Houston to a 110-109 lead, but Phoenix's Johnson was kneed and fouled after rebounding a Dan Majerle miss. He made the first foul shot with 21.6 seconds left -- his 21st in a row -- but missed the second.

Houston called time out with 20.4 seconds left and, when Phoenix trapped at midcourt, the ball was swung whimsically to Elie open in the corner. Schayes was the closest defender, guarding Olajuwon -- "It was either give up the jumper or let Hakeem have a dunk," Schayes said -- and so he let Elie airmail it.

"I've hit bigger shots," Elie said later. "Nah, just kidding."

results.title: From Poverty to the NBA: The Inspiring Journey of Africa's Basketball Star
results.description:
Before he was 'The Dream'... before he dominated the NBA... Hakeem Olajuwon was just a boy in Lagos, Nigeria, with a passion for soccer and no idea he would change basketball history.

In 1980, a 17-year-old Hakeem was discovered at a local basketball camp. Standing at 7 feet tall, his raw athleticism was undeniable. But he had never even heard of the NBA.  

He had no formal training, but his footwork—honed from soccer—was unlike anything we’d seen in a big man.  

With just two years of organized basketball under his belt, Hakeem enrolled at the University of Houston. Teaming up with Clyde Drexler, they formed 'Phi Slama Jama,' revolutionizing the game with high-flying dunks.

In 1984, Hakeem declared for the NBA Draft. The Houston Rockets selected him first overall—making him the first African player ever drafted in the NBA.  

The transition wasn’t easy. Critics doubted the 'project from Africa.' But Hakeem worked relentlessly, refining his legendary 'Dream Shake' and becoming a defensive terror.  

A decade after arriving in America, Hakeem Olajuwon wasn’t just the first African NBA player—he was its best. A two-time champion, MVP, and one of the greatest centers ever. 

His legacy? Proving greatness has no borders. And inspiring a continent to dream bigger.

New York Time : 1995 N.B.A. PLAYOFFS; Rockets Retire Suns, And Maybe Barkley
The Houston Rockets are on their ninth life, and Charles Barkley is about to get a life. A 3-point bomb from Houston's most obscure guard put the Rockets in victory lane today, and it also may have nudged one of basketball's most irascible players out the door.

His left knee creaks, his outside shot is flat and his Phoenix Suns revolve around somebody else, so Barkley announced late this afternoon that his retirement is imminent. He has said all of this before -- annually, in fact -- but today he went so far as to call a post-game meeting to tell his teammates that they can have his locker.

"I'm not saying this is 100 percent done, but I'll say more than likely I have played my last game," said Barkley, 32. "It's just time. It's time. I can't see my skills getting better; I can only see them getting worse."

Today, point guard Kevin Johnson borrowed the Suns from Barkley, scored 46 points, but watched in horror as the Rockets performed yet another magic trick to win, 115-114, in the seventh and final game of this Western Conference semifinal.

Mario Elie, who honed his shot at a park on the corner of 99th and Amsterdam in New York, stole the series by draining a 3-point corner shot with 7.1 seconds remaining.

"I told him he's a wicked man," Houston center Hakeem Olajuwon said of Elie.

It turned a 110-110 tie into a 113-110 Rockets lead and, after a Ping-Pong game of free throws, Danny Ainge's halfcourt heave at the buzzer -- to win it for Phoenix -- found only backboard.



Olajuwon was that center today, scoring 16 of his 29 points in the fourth quarter -- after serving as an assistant coach in the third. Not many clubs are as resilient as Houston. Two players in this series -- Clyde Drexler and Sam Cassell -- have needed I.V. treatment just to play, and two others -- the sharpshooter Vernon Maxwell (leave of absence) and power forward Carl Herrera (shoulder surgery) -- were watching back home.

"We could've gave up a lot of times," guard Kenny Smith said. "We could've given up today."

Instead, they defeated a team that had led this series by 3-1 and a player (A. C. Green) who had guaranteed victory after Game 4.

"Well, I have no words today," Green said. "It didn't happen. I've never experienced it before, so now I have something to describe in my next book."

Speaking of books, the Rockets will be inscribed in the league's history journal. They became only the fifth team to overcome a 3-1 deficit and the first team since the 1982 Sixers (who won in Boston) to win a seventh game on the road.

"Best team won," Phoenix's Johnson said. "We didn't deserve it. What's the excuse now? There is none, not when a team beats you three in a row, including twice at home."

Phoenix's halftime lead was 51-41, but Barkley had left the second quarter prematurely with a sore knee and reportedly took two shots of painkiller. He had started swiftly, with 8 points and 7 rebounds in the first quarter, but, in the second half, the most peculiar discussion occurred: Coach Paul Westphal told Ainge to tell Barkley that Johnson would be clearing out and going one on one against Smith on every possession.

Barkley rolled his eyes, but middle age was obviously setting in.

The third quarter was actually sailing along nicely -- the Suns were leading, 68-59, with Olajuwon on the bench with 5 minutes 25 seconds remaining -- when Drexler (29 points) awoke.

A 22-11 surge by Houston for the remainder of the quarter redirected the course of the game, and Coach Rudy Tomjanovich not once asked Olajuwon to budge.

"It gave me hope for the fourth quarter," Olajuwon said. "They'd taken us this far, and hopefully I could finish it."

Houston led, 81-79, entering the final quarter, and the only possession Olajuwon did not touch the ball was in the final 10 seconds. Phoenix was covering straight up with Joe Kleine or Danny Schayes, and Olajuwon was frothing at the mouth. He scored on fadeaways and layups -- until Phoenix had no choice but to triple-team him in the final two minutes.

With 45 seconds left, Smith made two free throws to elevate Houston to a 110-109 lead, but Phoenix's Johnson was kneed and fouled after rebounding a Dan Majerle miss. He made the first foul shot with 21.6 seconds left -- his 21st in a row -- but missed the second.

Houston called time out with 20.4 seconds left and, when Phoenix trapped at midcourt, the ball was swung whimsically to Elie open in the corner. Schayes was the closest defender, guarding Olajuwon -- "It was either give up the jumper or let Hakeem have a dunk," Schayes said -- and so he let Elie airmail it.

"I've hit bigger shots," Elie said later. "Nah, just kidding."

results.title: "It's a great feeling" Lillard on passing Drexler as Blazers' scoring leader
results.description:
Just when it appeared it might be “Dame Time,” Shai Gilgeous-Alexander stole the show.

Gilgeous-Alexander hit a baseline jumper as time expired, and the Oklahoma City Thunder defeated the Portland Trail Blazers 123-121 on Monday to ruin Damian Lillard's record-setting night.

Lillard had his clutch moment, too. He made a reverse layup with 3.5 seconds remaining to tie it, and finished with 28 points to break Clyde Drexler's franchise career scoring record.

Lillard would have preferred to set the mark in a win, but the achievement was still important to him.

“It’s a great feeling to reach the top,” he said. “It’s been a goal of mine and the list has so many players, great history of our organization, so to finally be No. 1 is a special accomplishment that I’m proud of.”

Drexler, a member of the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame, had 18,040 points for the Trail Blazers from 1983-95. Lillard entered the night needing 21 to pass him.

Lillard tied Drexler's total on a 3-pointer from well beyond the line in the third quarter that put the Trail Blazers up 72-67, then broke the mark on a free throw with 1:33 left in the period. Moments later, the Thunder public address announcer informed the crowd of Lillard’s achievement, and the crowd gave him an ovation. Lillard sat and rested, focused on a game the Trail Blazers were trailing by three points at the time.

results.title: 1992 NBA Finals Game 2 Portland Trail Blazers at Chicago Bulls, June 5, 1992, Clyde Ties the Series
results.description:
POR 115, CHI 104 - In Game 2 of the 1992 NBA Finals, the Portland Trail Blazers staged an incredible comeback to defeat Michael Jordan and the Chicago Bulls. Despite Jordan's stellar 39-point performance, the Blazers managed to overcome a daunting situation with less than five minutes remaining. Down 92-82 and missing Clyde Drexler, who had fouled out, Portland faced a loud crowd of 18,676 expecting another Bulls victory. However, the momentum shifted in the final nine minutes of the game.

Player of the game: 
Clyde Drexler: 26 PTS, 8-20 FGM, 10-10 FTM, 7 REB, 8 AST, 2 STL

Notable performance:
Michael Jordan: 39 PTS, 16-32 FGM, 7-9 FTM, 5 REB, 10 AST, 1 STL

Danny Ainge, stepping in for Drexler, scored nine of his 17 points in overtime, tying an NBA Finals record. His pivotal scoring and playmaking were vital for the Blazers, whose offense had struggled earlier in the series. Terry Porter also made a significant impact defensively, helping to limit Jordan's effectiveness and boosting the Blazers' overall performance. Meanwhile, the Bulls, despite having all five starters in double figures, faltered down the stretch. They missed three of their first six free throws in overtime and had difficulty finding good shots as the Blazers forced Jordan to pass.

The Bulls' defeat in Game 2 can be attributed to their overconfidence and excessive reliance on Michael Jordan, which led to a passive performance in the fourth quarter. This highlights a flaw in a heliocentric offense, where putting too much focus on one player can be detrimental. In contrast, the triangle offense was effective because it provided a more balanced approach, allowing every player on the floor the opportunity to be a playmaker or scorer, thus keeping everyone engaged in the game.

The Chicago Bulls lost their home-court advantage as the Portland Trail Blazers seized Game 2, leveling the series at 1-1. Although often seen as underdogs, the Blazers showcased their deep and experienced roster, proving they were a formidable challenge despite the overshadowing presence of Jordan and the Bulls.

Portland's lineup included All-Stars Clyde Drexler, Terry Porter, and Kevin Duckworth, along with Buck Williams, a formidable defender consistently considered for All-Defensive Teams and Defensive Player of the Year honors. The roster also featured the tenacious Jerome Kersey and Hall of Famer Danny Ainge. 

The Blazers finished the season first in the Western Conference with a 57-25 record, ranking third in Defensive Rating (104.2) and second in Net Rating (+7.3). For the second consecutive year, Portland claimed the top spot in the Western Conference.

The Blazers triumphed over the 43-39 Los Angeles Lakers in the first round, the 53-29 Phoenix Suns in the Semifinals, and the 55-27 Utah Jazz, led by Karl Malone and John Stockton, before facing the 67-15 defending champion Chicago Bulls in the NBA Finals.

results.description:

Michael Jordan delivered a performance for the ages, scoring 35 points in the first half alone, including six three-pointers — at a time when three-point shooting wasn’t his trademark. After burying his sixth triple, Jordan famously turned to the broadcast table and gave the “Jordan Shrug,” as if even he couldn’t believe it.

Jordan finished with 39 points and 11 assists, completely overwhelming Portland’s defense. Scottie Pippen added 24 points and 9 rebounds, while Horace Grant controlled the paint.

The Trail Blazers, led by Clyde Drexler (16 points, 5 rebounds) and Terry Porter (14 points, 7 assists), had no answers for Chicago’s offensive explosion. The Bulls dominated from start to finish, making a statement in the series opener.

📍 Final Score: Bulls 122 – Trail Blazers 89

New York Time : 1995 N.B.A. PLAYOFFS; Rockets Retire Suns, And Maybe Barkley
The Houston Rockets are on their ninth life, and Charles Barkley is about to get a life. A 3-point bomb from Houston's most obscure guard put the Rockets in victory lane today.

Today, point guard Kevin Johnson borrowed the Suns from Barkley, scored 46 points, but watched in horror as the Rockets performed yet another magic trick to win, 115-114, in the seventh and final game of this Western Conference semifinal.

Mario Elie, who honed his shot at a park on the corner of 99th and Amsterdam in New York, stole the series by draining a 3-point corner shot with 7.1 seconds remaining.

"I told him he's a wicked man," Houston center Hakeem Olajuwon said of Elie.

It turned a 110-110 tie into a 113-110 Rockets lead and, after a Ping-Pong game of free throws, Danny Ainge's halfcourt heave at the buzzer -- to win it for Phoenix -- found only backboard.



Olajuwon was that center today, scoring 16 of his 29 points in the fourth quarter -- after serving as an assistant coach in the third. Not many clubs are as resilient as Houston. Two players in this series -- Clyde Drexler and Sam Cassell -- have needed I.V. treatment just to play, and two others -- the sharpshooter Vernon Maxwell (leave of absence) and power forward Carl Herrera (shoulder surgery) -- were watching back home.

"We could've gave up a lot of times," guard Kenny Smith said. "We could've given up today."

Instead, they defeated a team that had led this series by 3-1 and a player (A. C. Green) who had guaranteed victory after Game 4.

"Well, I have no words today," Green said. "It didn't happen. I've never experienced it before, so now I have something to describe in my next book."

Speaking of books, the Rockets will be inscribed in the league's history journal. They became only the fifth team to overcome a 3-1 deficit and the first team since the 1982 Sixers (who won in Boston) to win a seventh game on the road.

"Best team won," Phoenix's Johnson said. "We didn't deserve it. What's the excuse now? There is none, not when a team beats you three in a row, including twice at home."

Phoenix's halftime lead was 51-41, but Barkley had left the second quarter prematurely with a sore knee and reportedly took two shots of painkiller. He had started swiftly, with 8 points and 7 rebounds in the first quarter, but, in the second half, the most peculiar discussion occurred: Coach Paul Westphal told Ainge to tell Barkley that Johnson would be clearing out and going one on one against Smith on every possession.

Barkley rolled his eyes, but middle age was obviously setting in.

The third quarter was actually sailing along nicely -- the Suns were leading, 68-59, with Olajuwon on the bench with 5 minutes 25 seconds remaining -- when Drexler (29 points) awoke.

A 22-11 surge by Houston for the remainder of the quarter redirected the course of the game, and Coach Rudy Tomjanovich not once asked Olajuwon to budge.
